cues.text: Alison Sharp has spent much of her life researching bears and in particular bears in danger of extinction. She is the author of a recent book on bears and we welcome her to the studio today.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Thank you. Delighted to be here.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: First of all, can you give us a quick overview of the history of the bear family?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Well, the bears we know today actually have as their ancestors bears which have been evolving for some 40 million years. We have fossils of the earliest 'true bear' - and it's important to emphasise this because some creatures are called bears but are not ...
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: ... such as koalas for instance.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes exactly ... fossils of the true bear show a small dog-size animal with characteristics that show a blending of dog and bear traits.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So the general belief is that dogs and bears were of the same family?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes, that's the theory. And then we see the arrival of the early Cave Bear. We know from cave drawings that Neanderthal man used to worship this bear and at the same time fear it.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Understandable perhaps ...
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes, but they need not have worried because the Cave Bear only ate plants. In fact the Cave Bear survived two Ice Ages but then became extinct.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So how many bears can we find today and are any of them in danger of extinction?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Well I'll answer your first question first. There are eight species of bear in all; among them the American Black Bear and the Brown Bear - from which evolved the newest species of bear - the Polar Bear.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So how old is the Polar Bear?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Oh, he's a relative newcomer - just 20,000 years old.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: And could you tell us a little about them? Which is the largest bear, for instance?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Well, the largest bear existing today is either the Polar Bear or the Brown Bear.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Right ... Don't we know?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Well, it depends which criteria you use. The Polar Bear is the heaviest; the male weighs up to 1,500 pounds but his narrow body actually makes him look smaller than the much more robust Brown Bear.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So the Brown Bear appears the biggest.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: And the smallest?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Well, the Sun Bear is the smallest of the eight species. They only weigh between 60 and 145 pounds.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: That makes him a comparative junior!
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes. And then next we have the so-called Giant Panda ... but that's a small bear too, comparatively speaking.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: And are all bears meat eaters?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: No, not at all. In fact the Giant Panda is almost entirely herbivorous living on a diet of 30 types of bamboo.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Oh, yes of course. Panda's are famous for that.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: And another interesting bear is the Sloth Bear which eats insects, particularly termites. He can turn his mouth into a tube and suck the insects out of their nests.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So going back to my second question ... Are bears really in danger of extinction?
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes indeed ... they are ... the Sun Bear in particular as they've been hunted almost out of existence. And the habitat of the Panda is also being reduced on a daily basis.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Can anything be done to reduce the threat to these endangered species? I know for instance that it's very hard to breed bears in captivity.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Yes, well ... I think that by raising people's awareness generally we can reduce conflict between humans and animals ...to stop the slaughter in parts of the world where bears are still hunted - supposedly in self- defense or to protect livestock, but ... often quite unnecessarily. And we can also encourage governments to preserve the natural environment of the bear rather than allow the areas where they live to be systematically destroyed in the name of progress.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Yes, of course.
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: And in addition to these global efforts, all profits from the sale of my book will go towards the United Nations Bear Protection program.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: That's wonderful ... and with the news coming up, thank you for your time, Alison, and best of luck with the book...
cues.speaker: Interviewer

cues.text: Thank you very much.
cues.speaker: Alison
